weeks.title: When Meaning Becomes Geometry

topics.title: Act I: The Magic, and the Map

concepts.title: Retrieval as the Epistemic Bottleneck
concepts.summary: Organisations fail not from lack of information but lack of retrievability — and a RAG generator can only be as truthful as the evidence placed before it.

concepts.title: Semantic vs Lexical Search & the Bi-Encoder
concepts.summary: Lexical search matches strings; semantic search matches meaning rendered as position in a vector space — the bi-encoder picture, and the three query families where they diverge.

concepts.title: The Map: Fourteen Instruments, One Pipeline
concepts.summary: The course is a single pipeline from raw document to measured, trustworthy answer — each week adds one instrument, and each instrument answers a specific pathology of naive RAG.

topics.title: Act II: How the Machine Sees

concepts.title: Language Models & the Seq2Seq Scaffold
concepts.summary: A language model factorises sequence probability into next-token predictions; seq2seq splits understanding (encoder) from speaking (decoder) — and RAG systems use two different models for the two jobs.

concepts.title: Attention: From Bahdanau's Alignment to 'All You Need'
concepts.summary: Attention began as a cure for the seq2seq bottleneck — soft alignment over encoder states — and the transformer made alignment the whole machine: a soft, differentiable lookup over keys and values.

concepts.title: Machines Think in 'Machinese': Vectors & Cosine Similarity
concepts.summary: The native currency of machine cognition is proximity, similarity, and probability — the distributional hypothesis, word2vec's directions of meaning, and why cosine similarity is the workhorse of retrieval.

concepts.title: Polysemy: One Word, Many Points
concepts.summary: Static embeddings strand ambiguous words between clusters; contextual embeddings read the sentence and move the point — and inside models, superposition is the same pressure one level deeper.

concepts.title: Querying Into the Model: LARQL & the Residual Stream
concepts.summary: A model's knowledge is geometry in its weights, and tools like LARQL can query it almost like a database — the doorway to mechanistic interpretability, and why a RAG engineer should never treat the model as an oracle.

topics.title: Act III: The Geometry of Meaning

concepts.title: Embeddings as Points in High-Dimensional Space
concepts.summary: An embedding model maps text to points in ℝᵈ where meaning is distributed holographically across coordinates; retrieval is nearest-neighbour search, made fast by ANN indexes like HNSW.

concepts.title: The Curse of Dimensionality
concepts.summary: As dimension grows, volume explodes, points become hopelessly sparse, and volume flees to the corners — the inscribed ball vanishes, naive spatial indexes degrade, and 'nearest' comes under pressure.

concepts.title: Concentration of Measure
concepts.summary: In high dimensions randomness becomes oddly orderly — pairwise distances concentrate, random vectors become nearly orthogonal, and useful structure must be put there by learning.

concepts.title: Anisotropy vs Isotropy: A Demonstration
concepts.summary: Concentration of measure is a property of the space; anisotropy is a property of the learned distribution within it — raw BERT embeddings crowd into a narrow cone, while retrieval-trained embeddings spread out and separate.

concepts.title: Naive RAG and Its Pathologies
concepts.summary: The simplest possible RAG system — embed, store, retrieve top-k, paste into the prompt — and a geometry-grounded catalogue of exactly how and why it fails.

weeks.title: The Shape of a Decision

topics.title: Act I: The Shape of a Decision

concepts.title: Softmax, Built by Hand — and the Temperature Knob
concepts.summary: The softmax turns a fistful of raw logits into a lawful probability distribution by exponentiating and normalizing, and one hidden knob, temperature, dials the result between a hard snap and a shrug without ever changing what the machine prefers.

concepts.title: Surprise, Negative Log-Likelihood, and the Cross-Entropy Family
concepts.summary: Surprise is a decreasing function of the probability you assigned to what actually happened, and the logarithm is the repair that sends certainty to zero surprise — from there, entropy, cross-entropy, and perplexity are just this one quantity, averaged and re-dressed.

concepts.title: Maximum Likelihood, the Gradient of Cross-Entropy, and Calibration
concepts.summary: Softmax paired with negative log-likelihood yields a gradient of disarming simplicity, predicted minus actual, and that same logarithm turns out to be forced rather than chosen — the only continuous repair that keeps a billion-term likelihood product computable at all.

topics.title: Act II: The Lookup That Learns

concepts.title: Attention as Fuzzy Dictionary Lookup: Four Exercises
concepts.summary: Attention is the fuzzy lookup you already perform every time you type a misspelled word into a dictionary — distribute a unit of attention over the nearby known words, weighted by proximity, and read off a blended meaning.

concepts.title: Tokenization, and Why Meaning Needs a Manifold
concepts.summary: A word is not the natural atom of text — a tokenizer chops it into subword pieces first — and machines must represent those pieces as points on a continuous manifold because gradient descent only ever makes infinitesimal moves.

concepts.title: Self-Attention Revisited: Query, Key, Value, and a Worked Example
concepts.summary: A word resolves its own ambiguity by scoring a query formed from itself against the keys of its sentence-mates and reading back a softmax-weighted blend of their values — the fuzzy dictionary lookup, turned inward and made differentiable.

concepts.title: Pooling, Layers, and the Residual Stream: From Tokens to One Vector
concepts.summary: Self-attention gives one contextual vector per token, but a search index wants one vector per chunk — mean-pooling bridges the gap, and stacking many attention layers over a residual stream is how that vector's meaning deepens.

concepts.title: Masked Language Modelling: Guess the Missing Word
concepts.summary: BERT's training objective is the card game of guessing a blanked-out word, scored by exactly the negative log-likelihood built this morning — and a model that consistently wins that game across billions of novel sentences must have learned something real about language.

topics.title: Act III: The Geometry of Belief

concepts.title: Anisotropy and Its Cure: Triplet Loss and InfoNCE
concepts.summary: A model trained only to predict words learns a representation crammed into a narrow cone, because attraction with no repulsion has one stable end state — contrastive learning supplies the missing repulsive force, and its modern form, InfoNCE, is the softmax and negative log-likelihood again, now sculpting the globe itself.

concepts.title: Bi-Encoders, Cross-Encoders, and the Unit Sphere
concepts.summary: There are exactly two ways to ask a BERT-like model how related two texts are, and the trade between them organizes the architecture of every retrieval system; both rely on cosine similarity, which is a dot product in disguise once vectors are normalized onto the unit sphere.

concepts.title: Search as Motion on a Curved Surface: KL Divergence, HNSW, and CLIP
concepts.summary: Once meaning is geometry, search is navigation across a curved surface — the same view that reveals KL divergence as the natural distance between beliefs, explains why a vector database walks a graph instead of scanning every point, and lets a sentence retrieve a photograph through CLIP's shared space.

weeks.title: Measuring the Size of Thoughts: To Chunk, or Not to Chunk?

topics.title: Act I: The First Cut Is the Deepest

concepts.title: The First Projection Is Irreversible
concepts.summary: Chunking is not preprocessing but the first lossy projection in the pipeline, and what the encoder never sees, the generator can never recover.

concepts.title: Why We Chunk: Atoms of Thought
concepts.summary: A document is an ensemble of thoughts, not one thought, and mixing two orthogonal ones in a single embedding creates a phantom point that answers neither.

concepts.title: The Boundary Problem and the 512-Token Default
concepts.summary: A document is a continuous stream of meaning with no ground-truth boundary, and the industry's default of 512 tokens is a baseline for expedience, not a considered choice.

topics.title: Act II: A Field Guide to What Chunking Destroys

concepts.title: Endophora and Broken References
concepts.summary: Language refers to itself through anaphora and cataphora, and cutting a chunk boundary between a pronoun and its antecedent leaves the fragment fluent but incoherent.

concepts.title: Discourse Structure and the Severing of Relations
concepts.summary: Documents are trees of rhetorical relations, not sequences of independent sentences, and severing them yields chunks that read true but mean the opposite of the whole.

concepts.title: The Negation Trap and Scope Failures
concepts.summary: Scope failures do not just lose information, they invert it, and presupposition accommodation silently promotes a hedged hypothesis to certainty with no error signal at all.

concepts.title: Lexical Cohesion and Definition–Use Chains
concepts.summary: Documents cohere through a sustained field of related words, and chunking dissolves that field, orphaning both disambiguating terms and legal definitions from their uses.

concepts.title: Bridging Inference and Genre Blindness
concepts.summary: Some connections have nothing explicit to sever, and a uniform chunk size ignores that a contract, a novel, and a paper carry information at wildly different densities.

concepts.title: Pathologies in Embedding Space
concepts.summary: A chunk's embedding is the centroid of its content, so packing distinct thoughts into one chunk produces a phantom vector near none of them, and anisotropy makes it worse.

topics.title: Act III: Two Roads — Better Chunking, or No Chunking?

concepts.title: A Taxonomy of Chunking Strategies
concepts.summary: From fixed-size to recursive to semantic to hierarchical chunking, each strategy improves where we cut but none heals what the cut severs.

concepts.title: Re-Contextualization: Contextual and Late Chunking
concepts.summary: Rather than inflate chunks, restore context dynamically — contextual chunking repairs in text space with an LLM-written preface, while late chunking repairs in latent space by chunking after encoding.

concepts.title: A Practical Pipeline
concepts.summary: The best systems layer markup, semantic hierarchy, contextualization, and late chunking as defense in depth, then let a tournament — not dogma — decide what to keep.

concepts.title: Road Two: Are We Barking Up the Wrong Tree?
concepts.summary: Every chunking strategy shares the hidden premise that we should parse text at all, and vision-language models like ColPali suggest that for layout-rich documents, the page image is the better semantic unit.

weeks.title: The Understudy: Search-Native Text & Derivative Artifacts

topics.title: Act I: The Purpose Problem

concepts.title: The Understudy: When the Text You Search Is Not the Text You Show
concepts.summary: For three weeks we indexed the author's own words; this week we manufacture new text written for the searcher, search that instead, and show the reader the original.

concepts.title: Meera and Ravi: Two Ways to Prepare for an Exam
concepts.summary: A story about two exam-takers shows that representation follows purpose, and that a textbook built for understanding is the wrong shape for a system that must instantly match a query to an answer.

concepts.title: Every Text Wears a Costume
concepts.summary: The same underlying fact is dressed differently for peer reviewers, adversaries, shareholders, and everyone else, and a user's naked query matches none of the costumes well.

concepts.title: The Central Provocation and the Geometry of Dilution
concepts.summary: The design principle for the rest of the week, plus the geometric reason it is necessary — a multi-claim paragraph embeds near the average of its claims, which dilutes its similarity to any one pointed query.

topics.title: Act II: The Derivative Artifacts — and the Proof

concepts.title: Factoids: Distilling the Atoms of Meaning
concepts.summary: A factoid is the smallest textual unit that still means something, the semantic molecule left after you pry every self-contained claim loose from a paragraph.

concepts.title: The PRML Bake-Off: Measuring the Difference
concepts.summary: A live experiment on Bishop's PRML textbook indexes raw chunks against factoids and QA pairs and asks why polynomial regression overfits, turning the week's claim from assertion into measurement.

concepts.title: The Centroid Tug-of-War: Feeling the Geometry
concepts.summary: A physical classroom demonstration with five students as fact-vertices and one marooned at their centroid makes the dilution inequality visible as a shrinking walk across the floor.

concepts.title: Passage Rewrites: The Source's Understudy
concepts.summary: A passage rewrite reformulates a hostile span into plain search-friendly language while the original clause remains the only thing ever shown to the reader or cited to the model.

concepts.title: QA Pairs: Planting Query-Shaped Objects
concepts.summary: Generating candidate questions per chunk turns retrieval into a same-genre match, question against question, instead of a cross-genre one, and a pointer back to the source keeps the artifact honest.

concepts.title: The Core Pattern: Retrieve the Derivative, Generate from the Source
concepts.summary: One pattern unifies every artifact in the toolkit — win the retrieval with the derivative but always generate and cite from the original, which bounds a bad derivative's damage to a missed retrieval, never a fabricated citation.

topics.title: Act III: Altitude — Summaries, RAPTOR, and the Corpus

concepts.title: Abstractive Summarization: Trading Detail for Altitude
concepts.summary: A summary is not a compression but a change of altitude, trading fine detail for large-scale structure and answering the thematic queries no single chunk can.

concepts.title: RAPTOR: Building the Zoom Lens
concepts.summary: RAPTOR gives summarization recursive structure, clustering and summarizing chunks over and over until a document becomes a tree searchable at every level of magnification.

concepts.title: From One Book to a Library: RAPTOR's Definitive Articles
concepts.summary: Run RAPTOR over a corpus rather than a document and its upper nodes stop summarizing one source, instead synthesizing a canonical answer across every document that touches the topic.

weeks.title: When the Library Becomes a City: GraphRAG

topics.title: Act I: The Mathematics of the City

concepts.title: Seven Bridges, One Sunday Walk: What a Graph Actually Is
concepts.summary: Euler's move on the bridges of Königsberg — discard geometry, keep connectivity — is the same move that turns a corpus into a knowledge graph.

concepts.title: The Adjacency Matrix: Where a Graph Becomes Calculable
concepts.summary: Numbering the vertices and recording edges as a matrix turns a drawing into something you can compute with — degree, walk counts, and every algorithm that follows.

concepts.title: Two Kinds of Randomness: Erdős–Rényi versus Barabási
concepts.summary: Fair-coin random graphs have no hubs; real networks do, because they grow by preferential attachment — and every knowledge graph inherits the same heavy tail.

concepts.title: Small Worlds and the Fractal-but-Real City
concepts.summary: Short paths plus tight clustering make a small world, and knowledge inherits the same self-similar, communities-within-communities architecture at a handful of real levels.

concepts.title: Communities, Modularity, and the Algorithm to Remember
concepts.summary: Modularity measures density-over-chance; Louvain optimizes it fast but can leave disconnected communities, and Leiden is the fix that Microsoft GraphRAG runs verbatim.

concepts.title: The Laplacian: One Definition, and a Door Left Ajar
concepts.summary: L = D − A measures how rough a score looks across a graph's edges — the same smoothing operator that reappears this afternoon as personalized PageRank.

topics.title: Act II: The Web of Knowledge — Triplets, Types, and Three Layers

concepts.title: Knowledge Is an Interconnected Web: Triplets and Their Types
concepts.summary: A knowledge graph is a bag of head-relation-tail triplets, and every fact triplet has a schema triplet standing behind it — the three-layer reading a corpus can be given.

concepts.title: Who Extracts: The Scooby-Doo Problem and Generic-Entity Hubs
concepts.summary: LLM extraction is cheap but indiscriminate, and the generic entities it inflates — United States, Person, Protein — become exactly the hubs Act I predicted, now with a name.

topics.title: Act III: The Many Meanings of GraphRAG

concepts.title: From Neighbor Expansion to Microsoft GraphRAG
concepts.summary: The oldest GraphRAG walks two hops from query entities and floods on hubs; Microsoft's 2024 pipeline instead harvests communities — at a real invoice.

concepts.title: The In-Betweens: LazyGraphRAG, LightRAG, and HippoRAG
concepts.summary: Three successors answer the invoice by deferring, slimming, or replacing community detection with personalized PageRank — the last one foreshadows tonight's centerpiece.

concepts.title: MemGraphRAG: Three Diseases and a Shared Memory
concepts.summary: MemGraphRAG diagnoses isolated fragment-level extraction as GraphRAG's root defect, then builds its graph by promoting only schemas whose frequency clears a threshold.

concepts.title: The Experiment: Running the Paper on Itself
concepts.summary: Running MemGraphRAG's own construction pipeline on a dozen passages of the paper itself produced a staircase of thresholds where no rung admits signal without noise.

concepts.title: Retrieval Without Communities: Three Cities of Lights and the Honey
concepts.summary: MemGraphRAG scores each layer's embeddings against the query, then lets that semantic energy diffuse via personalized PageRank — the Laplacian's diffusion, leashed and named.

concepts.title: Three Critiques, One Disease: Preserve, Then Decide
concepts.summary: MemGraphRAG indicts isolated extraction for destroying information, then commits the same sin three times at construction time — the fix is to defer judgment to query time.

topics.title: The Practitioner's Ledger: Patterns, Anti-Patterns, and the Sidecar

concepts.title: The Practitioner's Ledger: Patterns, Anti-Patterns, and the Sidecar
concepts.summary: GraphRAG is always a sidecar, never a replacement — it earns its keep on global sensemaking over a high-value sub-corpus, routed there by a local-versus-global query classifier.

weeks.title: The Two Gates of the Gatehouse: Guardrails, Grounding, Refusal & Humility

topics.title: Act I: The Gatehouse — Keeping Bad Questions Out

concepts.title: Two Gates, Two Virtues: Why RAG Needs Both
concepts.summary: A guardrailed RAG system needs two different gates guarding two different failures — a front gate that faces an adversary, and an exit gate that faces its own sincere machine.

concepts.title: Family A — Malformed and Evasive Input
concepts.summary: The model reads far more than your filters do, so an attacker who wants past a toxicity classifier simply encodes the message the more capable reader downstream will decode and obey.

concepts.title: Family B — Adversarial Intent
concepts.summary: There is no clean boundary between data and instructions in one token stream, so every prompt-injection defense is a way of re-drawing a boundary the architecture never had.

concepts.title: The RAG-Native Threat: Indirect Injection via Poisoned Retrieval
concepts.summary: The malicious instruction can lie dormant inside a document rather than the query, so the attacker never has to get past your gate at all — only into your index.

concepts.title: Family C — Access and Identity
concepts.summary: A query can be polite, on-topic, and injection-free and still be one this particular person must never have answered, because the failure is authorization, not content.

concepts.title: Family D — Abuse, Economics, and the Cheapest Structural Gate
concepts.summary: The last request-side family needs no forbidden word at all — it abuses the system by using it too much, spending its wallet, or exploiting its credulity — and one comparison operator, the length cap, retires most of it before a single classifier runs.

concepts.title: Giving the Gate a Memory: Duplicates, Keyword Stuffing, and Frustration
concepts.summary: Every gate so far judges one query in isolation and forgets it instantly — but a whole class of pattern, from repeated jailbreak attempts to a frustrated user, is only visible across a sequence of queries.

concepts.title: The Cheap First Gate: Domain Classification and the Toxicity Layer
concepts.summary: One cheap classifier asking 'is this even about our domain?' silently absorbs most off-topic malice for free, and a dedicated toxicity layer catches the on-topic malice the domain gate cannot see.

concepts.title: The False-Positive Tax, and Orchestrating the Gatehouse
concepts.summary: A suspicious posture is right at any single gate, but false-positive rates compound across a deep stack until the gatehouse quietly turns away one legitimate user in six.

topics.title: Act II: The Conscience — Keeping Bad Answers In

concepts.title: The Wizard's Curtain: Groundedness, Faithfulness, and the RAGAS Triad
concepts.summary: A RAG system speaks in the same confident voice whether or not there's real evidence behind it, so groundedness measures — claim by claim — whether the confidence was earned.

concepts.title: The Assertion–Evidence Bipartite Graph
concepts.summary: Turning the faithfulness definition into a graph — claims on one side, evidence on the other — turns a vague verdict of 'this answer seems off' into a pointer at the exact offending sentence.

concepts.title: Two Verifiers and the Escalation Ladder of Conscience
concepts.summary: An LLM judge is smarter than the cheap NLI model but carries its own documented biases, so production conscience is a cost-ordered cascade that spends the expensive verifier only on the residue the cheap one couldn't settle.

concepts.title: Citation Faithfulness, Caught Hallucinations, and Who Guards the Guard
concepts.summary: A citation is itself a claim that can be false — and detecting a hallucination is worthless without a policy for what to do with it, which is where Act II confronts the recursive limits of its own machinery.

topics.title: Act III: Refusal and Humility

concepts.title: Refusal Is a First-Class Output: The Three Doors, and Why Humility Is Graded
concepts.summary: Sometimes the honest output is no output at all — but refusal is a binary values decision through one of three doors, while humility is the graded, epistemic skill of saying how much of the rest is actually known.

concepts.title: Verbalized Uncertainty: The Linguistics of an Honest Hedge
concepts.summary: A hedge is only honest if a real, measured signal sits underneath it — which rules out both a fake-precise confidence number and the model's own self-report of how sure it is.

concepts.title: Conformal Abstention, Calibration, and the Positive Conscience
concepts.summary: Conformal prediction turns a raw uncertainty score into a threshold with a provable, distribution-free error-rate guarantee — and the whole ethic of the week is stating that error rate out loud instead of guessing at it.

topics.title: Laboratory Sessions

concepts.title: Laboratory Sessions: What We Build and Measure
concepts.summary: Eight labs turn this week's intuition into a deployed artifact in front of a real RAG system, building the gatehouse first, then the conscience, then the honest refusal — and measuring every detector rather than trusting it on faith.

weeks.title: The Measure of All Things: Evaluation and the Search Mind

topics.title: Act I: Evaluation and the Search Mind

concepts.title: The Measure of All Things: Evaluation and the Search Mind
concepts.summary: A retrieval system is only as good as the test it survives; this week makes evaluation part of the architecture, not an afterthought.

concepts.title: Ranking Is Not the Same as Utility
concepts.summary: A system can rank the right facts highly and still fail the user because the task is not about ranking alone but about usefulness under constraints.

concepts.title: The Benchmark Trap and the Contaminated Mirror
concepts.summary: The hardest evaluation problem is not a bad model; it is a benchmark that has already seen the answer.

weeks.title: The Library in Your Head: Memory, Context, and Retrieval

topics.title: Act I: Memory, Context, and Retrieval

concepts.title: Memory, Context, and Retrieval
concepts.summary: The system's memory is not just a database; it is the context layer that decides which facts are worth reusing and which are just noise.

concepts.title: The Context Window as a Tradeoff
concepts.summary: A context window is not a free resource. It is a bounded memory budget that trades breadth, depth, and latency against one another.

concepts.title: Episodic Memory and Semantic Memory
concepts.summary: A useful assistant needs both remembered events and stable facts; the difference between them determines how memory should be retrieved.

weeks.title: Entitlement-Aware Retrieval and the Library of Many Catalogues

topics.title: Act I: Entitlement-Aware Retrieval and the Library of Many Catalogues

concepts.title: Entitlement-Aware Retrieval
concepts.summary: Not every user should see every document; the retrieval layer must respect permission, role, and access boundaries.

concepts.title: Permission as a Retrieval Constraint
concepts.summary: A retrieval system must treat permission as a first-class constraint, not a downstream check.

concepts.title: Role-Typed Retrieval and Tenant Isolation
concepts.summary: Users do not only differ by query. They differ by role, scope, and trust boundary, and the retrieval stack must respect that.

weeks.title: The Room as the Corpus: Place, Memory, and Shared Context

topics.title: Act I: The Room as the Corpus

concepts.title: Place, Memory, and Shared Context
concepts.summary: Some retrieval systems are about a document corpus; others are about a shared room of people, memory, and interaction.

concepts.title: Shared Memory and Session State
concepts.summary: The memory of a system is not only eternal; it is also the state of the current room, the current task, and the current session.

concepts.title: Temporal Context and Place
concepts.summary: The same document has different meanings depending on when it is retrieved and in what room it is being used.

weeks.title: Cachecraft, Shareability, and the Searchable Commons

topics.title: Act I: Cachecraft, Shareability, and the Searchable Commons

concepts.title: Cachecraft, Shareability, and the Searchable Commons
concepts.summary: The final week asks how knowledge is cached, shared, and reused across users, systems, and organizations.

concepts.title: Caching for Common Queries
concepts.summary: Repeated retrieval work should not always be recomputed; good caching is a system design decision, not an optimization afterthought.

concepts.title: Governance, Freshness, and Shared Knowledge
concepts.summary: A shared retrieval system must be governed by freshness, provenance, and policy so that reuse does not turn into drift.

weeks.title: The Three Pillars and the Shape of an Agent

topics.title: Act I: Why Agents, Why Now

concepts.title: The Holy Trinity: Agents, RAG, and Fine-Tuning
concepts.summary: Successful enterprise AI is built on three interconnected pillars — intelligent agents, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning — and neglecting any one produces a brittle system.

concepts.title: The Pot of Milk: Why POCs Never Reach Production
concepts.summary: A folktale about a king's vessel of "milk" that turned out to be water explains why so many corporate agentic teams produce impressive demos that never survive contact with reality.

concepts.title: The Case for Small: Fine-Tuned Specialists vs. Frontier Generalists
concepts.summary: A fine-tuned small language model in the 30-70B range will consistently outperform a prompted frontier model on a specific domain task, at a fraction of the long-run cost.

topics.title: Act II: What Is An Agent

concepts.title: The Observe-Reason-Act Loop
concepts.summary: An AI agent is formally defined by a repeating cycle — observe the environment, reason about a plan, act to change the environment's state — that continues until the goal is recognized as met.

concepts.title: Agents, Programs, and the Trap of Programming in English
concepts.summary: Programs and workflows execute explicit, hardwired instructions; agents are given a goal and reason autonomously about how to reach it — and micromanaging an agent with step-by-step instructions is a contradiction in terms.

concepts.title: Agent or Tool? The Reusability Test
concepts.summary: Whether a function using an LLM is an "agent" or merely a "tool" hinges on reusability, not on whether it invokes a language model — and the distinction is contextual, since agents can themselves serve as tools to other agents.

topics.title: Act III: Reliability, Memory, and the Agentic World

concepts.title: Memory, Critique, and Reflection: The Rubric for Reliable Agents
concepts.summary: An agent without memory resembles a person with dementia, unable to build on prior context; critique and self-reflection exploit the fact that an LLM's discriminative ability usually exceeds its generative ability, giving agents a practical way to catch their own mistakes.

concepts.title: Frameworks, MCP, and Agents in the Wild
concepts.summary: Orchestration frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI) evolve fast and should hold only a thin integration layer; MCP standardizes tool access as a "USB port for agents"; and agentic systems already run dark factories, seaports, and Mars rover landings.

weeks.title: From Genie to Prompt: Anatomy and Voice

topics.title: Act I: The Anatomy of an Agent

concepts.title: The Anatomy of an Agent, Revisited
concepts.summary: An agent's five components — environment, goal, observation, reasoning, action — combine with a specific historical breakthrough in autonomous reasoning, without which the whole architecture stays theoretical.

concepts.title: The Contextual Hierarchy: You Are an Agent, and Also a Tool
concepts.summary: Whether something is an agent or a tool is relative to the observer's level in a hierarchy — an agent to itself can be a tool to whatever orchestrates it, a pattern that scales complex multi-agent systems the same way organizations scale human ones.

concepts.title: Environment Fencing and the Documentation Bottleneck
concepts.summary: At enterprise scale, agent reliability breaks down not from weak models but from poorly written tool documentation and unfenced overlap between similar tools — and the fix is often disappointingly non-technical.

topics.title: Act II: Reasoning, Learning, and Memory

concepts.title: Learning, Memorization, and Why Agents Can't Learn on the Fly (Yet)
concepts.summary: True learning bakes a behavioral change permanently into a model's weights; RAG-based memorization retrieves facts on demand without changing the model at all — and continuous online learning remains impractical because training costs roughly four times what inference costs.

concepts.title: Ambient and Embodied Agents: Intelligence Without Being Asked
concepts.summary: Ambient agents observe passively and act only on specific triggers, unlike interactive agents that wait for a prompt; embodied agents extend reasoning into physical actuation, and the distinguishing test for both is whether genuine reasoning — not mechanical rule-firing — sits behind the response.

topics.title: Act III: Prompt Engineering as Agent Design

concepts.title: CO-STAR and the Thousand PhDs Behind the Curtain
concepts.summary: An LLM behaves like a thousand experts behind a curtain, and a system prompt is how you summon a specific one — the CO-STAR framework (Context, Objective, Style, Tone, Audience, Response format) structures that summoning into something precise and repeatable.

concepts.title: The Old Faithful Case Study: What a Prompt Can Actually Unlock
concepts.summary: A single, carefully structured prompt turned an early-2023 GPT model into an autonomous data scientist that performed and interpreted an entire exploratory analysis unassisted — proof that role-based prompting activates dormant capability rather than teaching new skill.

weeks.title: You Cannot Improve What You Cannot Measure

topics.title: Act I: Measurement as the Foundation

concepts.title: The Axiom of Measurement: You Cannot Improve What You Cannot Measure
concepts.summary: The single most common failure mode in agent development is testing on one or two examples and deploying — an agent is a system whose quality can only be established by systematically comparing outputs against known-correct results, exactly like any supervised model.

concepts.title: Gold Standard Datasets and the Product Manager as Data Architect
concepts.summary: A gold-standard dataset of diverse, hard, large-n task-result pairs is the actual specification for an agent, and it re-defines the product manager's job as building that specification rather than writing feature specs — with the test set held back from the engineers who build the prompt.

topics.title: Act II: The Prompting Toolkit

concepts.title: Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Why Chain-of-Thought Became a Bad Idea
concepts.summary: Zero-shot and few-shot prompting remain broadly useful, but chain-of-thought prompting — once essential before genuine reasoning models existed — is now counterproductive for reasoning models, because it shackles a model that has figured out a better way to think.

concepts.title: ReAct and Reflexion: Closing the Loop Between Thinking and Refining
concepts.summary: ReAct bridges pure prompting to genuine agentic behavior by interleaving reasoning and acting; Reflexion adds a self-refinement loop on top, and the pair-agent pattern (editor / senior editor) operationalizes it with an explicit checklist rather than a vague "do better.

concepts.title: Never Trust Raw Input: The Query Transformer Agent
concepts.summary: The first agent in any agentic workflow should be a query transformer that rationalizes typos, expands acronyms via RAG, standardizes named entities, and rewrites the query into a clean form — a user-proxy step that protects every downstream agent from the mess of real human language.

topics.title: Act III: Economics and Engineering Discipline

concepts.title: The Model Tournament: Choosing SLMs with Data, Not Opinion
concepts.summary: Rather than debating model choice opinion by opinion, run a systematic tournament — optimize a prompt per candidate model, measure error rates empirically, and let the data pick the winner before fine-tuning it further.

concepts.title: The Middle Path: AI-Assisted Coding Without Vibe Coding
concepts.summary: Between complete vibe coding and refusing to use AI code generators at all lies a disciplined middle path — Cursor Rules that encode a team's standards as persistent, machine-readable constraints, converting an AI code generator into a reliable, opinionated assistant.

weeks.title: The Stochastic Parrot and the Reliability Crisis

topics.title: Act I: The Reliability Crisis

concepts.title: The Stochastic Parrot: Sampling, Temperature, and Why Zero Isn't Zero
concepts.summary: LLMs are next-token prediction engines that sample from a probability distribution rather than always picking the most likely word — and temperature, the user-facing knob that controls this, is quietly log-transformed so that even setting it to zero never fully removes randomness.

concepts.title: The Enterprise Reliability Crisis: Two Axioms in Collision
concepts.summary: The whole crisis facing agentic adoption reduces to two axioms colliding — LLMs underlie agents, and LLMs are inherently stochastic — and the course's contention is that this crisis is a mirage caused by immature system architecture, not an unsolvable property of the technology.

topics.title: Act II: Architecting Reliable Agents

concepts.title: The Tool-Maximalist Perspective: Intelligence Is Not in the Model Alone
concepts.summary: Under the tool-maximalist view, an agent's intelligence emerges from the ecosystem of reasoner plus tools, not from the model's weights in isolation — and MCP is the protocol that lets tools describe their own capabilities richly enough for an agent to reason about what's possible before deciding how to act.

concepts.title: Single Agent, Many Tools: Text-to-SQL as a Microcosm
concepts.summary: The single-agent-multiple-tools architecture is often the right starting point, chosen by context rather than fashion (a "no free lunch theorem" for agentic architectures) — and text-to-SQL is the clearest small-scale demonstration of both the breathtaking promise and the genuine difficulty of the whole agentic paradigm.

concepts.title: Plan First: The Cursor Template for Agent Behavior
concepts.summary: The first thing a well-behaved agent should do is itemize a task list before acting — the exact pattern visible in coding assistants like Cursor — converting an opaque single-shot generation into a visible, checkable, revisable plan.

concepts.title: The Reliability Toolkit: Caching, Guardrails, Evals, and Cross-Verification
concepts.summary: No single technique resolves the enterprise reliability crisis; semantic caching, human-in-the-loop review, guardrails, golden datasets, and multi-agent cross-verification each attack a different piece of it, and the right combination depends on where a specific task's stochasticity actually causes harm.

weeks.title: Agents, Tools, and the Machinery Between Them

topics.title: Act I: Agent or Tool? The Litmus Test

concepts.title: The Litmus Test: Agent or Tool?
concepts.summary: The only reliable way to decide whether a piece of functionality should be an Agent or a Tool is to ask whether it needs inference-time reasoning — everything else is a naming argument.

concepts.title: Dressing an Agent Up as a Tool
concepts.summary: When a reasoning-heavy function is genuinely reusable, the best practice is to expose it through a plain Tool interface — hiding the agent inside so other agents and teams can call it without understanding its internals.

topics.title: Act II: Knowledge Graphs as an Agent's Domain Memory

concepts.title: Centrality: Why Structure Beats Frequency
concepts.summary: A keyword extractor that ranks by how central a term is in a domain's knowledge graph, rather than by raw frequency, surfaces the terms that actually matter to a domain — frequency is only a tiebreaker.

concepts.title: The Knowledge Graph as Capital Investment
concepts.summary: A domain knowledge graph pays for itself across every downstream application — glossaries, retrieval, categorization, diagnostics — because it is a slow-moving, reusable capital asset rather than a one-off analysis.

topics.title: Act III: From Prototype to Production — MCP Architecture

concepts.title: MCP: Making Tools Legible to a Model
concepts.summary: The Model Context Protocol standardizes how a tool describes itself so an LLM-backed agent can discover, understand, and safely invoke it — and its reach extends past software into physical systems.

concepts.title: Three Levels of MCP Maturity: Direct, Gateway, Ray
concepts.summary: MCP tool deployment matures through three stages — direct, gateway, and Ray-backed — mirroring the historical evolution of web servers, because AI workloads reintroduce exactly the isolation and scaling problems that mature server architecture already solved once.

concepts.title: Resolving the Agent Intelligence Paradox
concepts.summary: Agent servers need to be scaled like dumb, stateless applications while the LLMs powering them need specialized inference infrastructure — the resolution is to keep agents thin and delegate all model serving to a dedicated layer like vLLM inside the same Ray cluster.

weeks.title: The Physics of Scale and Cooperation

topics.title: Act I: Frameworks and the Physics of Scale

concepts.title: CrewAI vs. LangGraph: Two Philosophies, One Fatal Flaw
concepts.summary: CrewAI and LangGraph represent different philosophies of agent orchestration — magical automation versus explicit graph control — but both share the same fatal flaw when a workflow's structure can't be known in advance.

concepts.title: Engineering Is Never Scale-Invariant
concepts.summary: Galileo's Square-Cube Law and Amdahl's Law both say the same thing about agentic systems in different registers — the right architecture depends on scale, and a system's speed is capped by its single slowest link.

concepts.title: The Insane Extravaganza: Right-Sizing the Model
concepts.summary: Most calls to frontier LLMs are for trivial tasks a tiny model could handle a thousand times faster — the fix is a hybrid architecture where a rules engine routes atomic tasks to the smallest model that can do the job.

topics.title: Act II: When Agents Must Talk to Other Agents

concepts.title: Levels of Autonomy: From Operator to Observer
concepts.summary: Agentic systems exist on a graded scale of autonomy, and internal multi-agent orchestration (one process, many sub-agents) is a fundamentally different problem from external multi-agent communication across organizational boundaries.

concepts.title: A2A: Discovery Is the Whole Problem
concepts.summary: Agent-to-Agent communication has to solve the same discovery problem the internet solved with DNS, and today's peer-to-peer Agent Cards are a known-good-enough solution, not the long-term one.

concepts.title: When the Adversary Is Another Agent
concepts.summary: Multi-agent systems face security threats beyond traditional API security — impersonation, model poisoning, and prompt injection at the agent-to-agent boundary — and the tool-vs-service distinction determines what kind of trust each interaction actually requires.

topics.title: Act III: Agentic RAG — When Retrieval Needs a Planner

concepts.title: Why Bigger Context Windows Didn't Kill RAG
concepts.summary: Million-token context windows tempted people to declare RAG dead, but cost, latency, the lost-in-the-middle effect, and quadratic attention complexity all argue for retrieving less, more precisely, rather than stuffing everything in.

concepts.title: Semantic Cache and Exploratory Search
concepts.summary: Because human language is elastic but questions repeat, a semantic cache can turn 95%+ of enterprise queries into near-instant lookups — and an agent that searches, evaluates, and re-searches mimics how humans actually refine a question.

concepts.title: Response Grounding, and What Storm Knows That LangGraph Doesn't
concepts.summary: A response-side guardrail agent must check grounding, relevance, completeness, and toxicity before an answer reaches a user — and Stanford's Storm system shows what a genuinely dynamic, plan-from-scratch agentic system looks like, in contrast to LangGraph's a priori graphs.

weeks.title: Why and When to Fine-Tune an Agent

topics.title: Act I: Why Machines Need Training At All

concepts.title: What Training Actually Is: Chasing an Unknown Function
concepts.summary: Model training is the search for a function f(x) that approximates an unknown ground-truth function g(x) — a framing that unifies ice-cream sales forecasting, cow-vs-duck classification, and every large language model into one idea.

concepts.title: The Guessing Game That Teaches Language
concepts.summary: Foundational models learn broad ability through surrogate tasks — artificial games with no direct utility of their own — that force the model to develop general understanding as a side effect of playing them well.

topics.title: Act II: Fine-Tuning vs Prompting vs RAG

concepts.title: The Actor Handed a Script vs. the Actor Who Became the Role
concepts.summary: Prompting gives a model a script to improvise from fresh on every call; fine-tuning changes what the model fundamentally is — and that distinction, not model size, is why "agents" built purely on prompts earn the criticism that they're unreliable.

concepts.title: The Escalation Ladder, and Why Fine-Tuning Is Never for Knowledge
concepts.summary: A mature system escalates from prompt to RAG to fine-tuning only as needed — and fine-tuning should almost never be used to store knowledge, because an LLM's weights are a lossy, uncitable memory while RAG offers verifiable, retrievable evidence.

concepts.title: The Web of Models: Specialization vs. Scale
concepts.summary: The debate between one large frontier model and a distributed web of small fine-tuned specialists comes down to OPEX vs. CAPEX, the Mixture-of-Experts specialization trap, and whether 2 + 2 can genuinely be made to exceed 4.

topics.title: Act III: Designing Agents That Plan, Fail, and Reflect

concepts.title: Beyond ReAct: Planning, Re-Planning, and Reflection
concepts.summary: A bare ReAct loop errors out when it hits max_retries with no recovery path — planning, re-planning, and reflection are three design patterns that add resilience by letting an agent revise its own plan or judge its own output quality.

concepts.title: The Patient Advocate: An Agent That Must Not Play Doctor
concepts.summary: The patient-advocacy agent project forces every design pattern from this week — planning, tool calling, statefulness — through a single hard constraint: guide, never diagnose, using the SOAP framework as the structuring principle.

weeks.title: The Surgery of Fine-Tuning

topics.title: Act I: The Anatomy and Risk of Fine-Tuning

concepts.title: Two Reasons to Fine-Tune, and When Not To
concepts.summary: Fine-tuning is justified by domain adaptation (a new dialect) or task specificity (a new objective), and the same escalation logic that says "reach for it last" also says "check whether you have a transferable skill to leverage before training from scratch.

concepts.title: Knowing When to Stop: The Acceptance Threshold
concepts.summary: Fine-tuning needs a metric, a realistic evaluation dataset, and an agreed acceptance threshold defined before training starts — because fine-tuning is a constrained optimization problem where "more training" is not automatically better.

concepts.title: Fine-Tuning Is Neurosurgery, Not a Coding Task
concepts.summary: Fine-tuning is a constrained optimization problem, not an unconstrained one — the goal is to meet a performance bar with the least damage to existing capability, because catastrophic forgetting and mode collapse are the price paid for every parameter update.

topics.title: Act II: Surgical Fine-Tuning — From Full Updates to LoRA

concepts.title: Which Layers Actually Need Surgery
concepts.summary: Full model fine-tuning updates every parameter at a roughly 3.6x memory cost and high forgetting risk, while representation learning theory and gradient heatmaps let you identify and update only the specific layers that actually need to change.

concepts.title: LoRA: The Small Change That Doesn't Touch the Original
concepts.summary: LoRA freezes the entire base model and learns only a small, low-rank perturbation alongside it — a rudder steering a frozen engine rather than rebuilding the engine, which is why adapters are cheap, fast, and stackable.

concepts.title: From SaaS to DeepSeek: How Fine-Tuning Actually Gets Shipped
concepts.summary: Practical fine-tuning splits into SaaS platforms and code-based approaches, base vs. instruct models present a real starting-point trade-off, and DeepSeek's published pipeline shows mode collapse being deliberately induced and then deliberately repaired within one training run.

topics.title: Act III: Trust at the System Level

concepts.title: MCP, A2A, and the Missing DNS for Agents
concepts.summary: MCP handles agent-to-tool, A2A handles agent-to-agent, and neither solves directory-based discovery at internet scale — the Linux Foundation's Agency project is an attempt to build exactly that missing layer.

concepts.title: Pinning Every Claim to Its Evidence
concepts.summary: Grounding a RAG answer means decomposing it into individual factoids and pinning each to specific retrieved evidence — and rising token-level entropy during generation is a real-time signal that the model is about to hallucinate.

weeks.title: The Escalation Ladder: Prompting to Reinforcement Learning

topics.title: Act I: The Escalation Ladder for Agent Intelligence

concepts.title: The Four Pillars: Prompting, Cooperation, Tools, and Training
concepts.summary: An agent's strength comes from four independent levers — prompting, multi-agent cooperation, tools, and training — and confusing which lever is weak is the most common way agent projects stall.

concepts.title: Defining the Agent: An Autonomous Reasoner Empowered by Tools
concepts.summary: An agent is an autonomous reasoner given a goal, an environment, and a set of tools — and it is the tools, not raw reasoning, that most often set the ceiling on what it can accomplish.

concepts.title: Training Has Two Jobs: Core Competency and Cooperation
concepts.summary: Fine-tuning an agent for individual skill and fine-tuning it to cooperate with teammates are two different training goals requiring two different methodologies — and confusing them stalls multi-agent projects.

concepts.title: The Escalation Ladder: Climb Only as Far as You Must
concepts.summary: Solve agent problems with the cheapest sufficient technique first — prompting, then prompt optimization, then model size, then RAG, then supervised fine-tuning, then reinforcement learning — because each rung costs more and reaches fewer people.

concepts.title: The Fundamental Dichotomy: Knowledge Versus Reasoning
concepts.summary: RAG and fine-tuning solve two different problems — RAG injects knowledge the model lacks, fine-tuning instills reasoning or strategy the model cannot derive from any document — and picking the wrong one is the most expensive mistake on the escalation ladder.

concepts.title: The Pareto Frontier: CapEx, OpEx, and the RAG-Versus-Fine-Tuning Trade
concepts.summary: RAG and fine-tuning sit at different points on a CapEx-versus-OpEx Pareto frontier, and the right choice is not "which is better" but "which point on the frontier matches your traffic volume.

weeks.title: The Vocabulary of Reinforcement Learning

topics.title: Act I: The Vocabulary of Reinforcement Learning

concepts.title: Two Parenting Styles: What Actually Distinguishes Reinforcement Learning
concepts.summary: Supervised learning hands the learner a ground-truth answer for every input; reinforcement learning hands it only a goal and a reward, and the difference in what the learner discovers on its own is the whole story of RL.

concepts.title: Agent, Environment, State, Action, Episode: The Core Vocabulary
concepts.summary: Every reinforcement learning system, from a Roomba to a language model, is described by the same five nouns — agent, environment, state, action, episode — and learning to see them everywhere is the actual skill this week teaches.

concepts.title: The Value of a State, and Why the Actor Needs a Critic
concepts.summary: The value of a state is the expected reward of every trajectory starting there, and separating a Critic that judges states from an Actor that picks actions is the architectural move that makes learning tractable.

concepts.title: The Policy as a Theory of the World, and Why Rewards Get Discounted
concepts.summary: A policy is the agent's internal theory of what action a state calls for, and discounting future rewards is the mathematical device that stops a policy from confusing a slow win with a fast one — or from looping forever to farm small rewards.

concepts.title: Long-Term Strategy: What Move 37 and AlphaFold Actually Proved
concepts.summary: AlphaGo's Move 37 and AlphaFold's protein-folding breakthrough are the same proof, twice — that optimizing over whole trajectories rather than local steps lets reinforcement learning discover strategies no human ever demonstrated.

concepts.title: Mapping Reinforcement Learning onto Language Models
concepts.summary: A language model is a reinforcement-learning agent in disguise — the prompt-plus-generated-tokens is the state, the next token is the action, and the whole model is the policy — and this mapping is what makes training LLMs with RL possible at all.

weeks.title: Inside Manus, and the Mathematics of Policy Gradients

topics.title: Act I: Inside Manus

concepts.title: Context Engineering for AI Agents: Lessons from Building Manus
concepts.summary: Manus bet on context engineering over training a custom model, and its six hard-won rules — cache design, masking over removal, filesystem-as-memory, recitation, keeping failures visible, and avoiding few-shot ruts — are load-bearing production lessons, not style preferences.

concepts.title: Inside Manus: CodeAct, the Sandbox, and the Agent Loop
concepts.summary: Manus is not a proprietary model but an orchestration layer around frontier LLMs, made powerful by three architectural choices — executable code as the action format, a full cloud sandbox, and a strictly one-action-per-iteration control loop.

concepts.title: Externalized Memory, Recitation, and Productive Failure
concepts.summary: Long-running agents fight three problems no context window fixes on its own — running out of room, forgetting the goal, and losing the evidence of their own mistakes — and the filesystem, a recited todo list, and an intact error trace solve all three.

topics.title: Act II: The Risks Beneath the Escalation Ladder

concepts.title: The Sand Analogy: Why Fine-Tuning Can Break What It Doesn't Touch
concepts.summary: Fine-tuning nudges a probability distribution rather than replacing it, and pushed too hard it borrows probability mass from abilities you never meant to touch — producing catastrophic forgetting and mode collapse that show up in surprising, specific ways.

concepts.title: From Consequence to Causation: The Log-Derivative Trick and REINFORCE
concepts.summary: You cannot differentiate a discrete outcome, but you can differentiate the continuous cause behind it — the log-derivative trick is the single identity that turns "make good tokens more likely" into a computable gradient, and it is the entire mathematical seed of REINFORCE.

weeks.title: Trust Regions and the Reasoning Breakthrough

topics.title: Act I: Trust Regions and the Reasoning Breakthrough

concepts.title: KL Divergence: Measuring How Far a Policy Has Drifted
concepts.summary: KL divergence measures how much one probability distribution fails to look like another, derived from a simple coin-toss likelihood-ratio argument, and it becomes the mathematical tether that keeps policy updates from wandering too far from where they started.

concepts.title: Trust Region Policy Optimization: The Lakshman Rekha for Policy Updates
concepts.summary: A policy update that maximizes reward without limit can collapse the model that produced it — TRPO constrains every update to stay within a KL-divergence trust region, formalizing the intuition of a soldier who never strays too far from base camp.

concepts.title: Proximal Policy Optimization: Tiny Feet Instead of Exact Trust Regions
concepts.summary: PPO keeps TRPO's stabilizing intuition but replaces its expensive exact KL constraint with a cheap clipped probability ratio — tiny feet instead of precise geometry — and that simplification is what made it the algorithm that actually trained ChatGPT.

concepts.title: The InstructGPT Pipeline: How SFT, a Reward Model, and PPO Built ChatGPT
concepts.summary: ChatGPT is not one training run but three chained steps — supervised demonstrations, a learned reward model standing in for human judgment, and PPO optimizing against that reward — and the seams between those steps are exactly where reward hacking gets in.

concepts.title: DeepSeek-R1: Reasoning from Pure RL, and Group Relative Policy Optimization
concepts.summary: DeepSeek-R1-Zero dropped the reward model and the SFT warm-start entirely, rewarding only verifiable correctness on math and code, and GRPO's group-relative Z-score let reasoning emerge from pure reinforcement learning rather than imitation.

concepts.title: The Geometry of SFT vs. RL: Why One Breaks the Model and the Other Doesn't
concepts.summary: SFT updates a model along its highest-curvature, most structurally load-bearing directions, risking catastrophic collapse; RL updates it along low-curvature, structure-preserving directions instead — a geometric answer to why RL is safer despite being slower.

weeks.title: Coordinating Many Minds: Multi-Agent RL

topics.title: Act I: Coordinating Many Minds

concepts.title: Distributed AI and the Fallacy of the Super Genius
concepts.summary: A multi-agent system succeeds by assembling many hyper-specialized one-trick-pony agents, not by searching for one universal super-genius model, because the required skill combinations are frequently contradictory within a single trained policy.

concepts.title: The Economics of Agentic Systems: Latency, Cost, and the Van Gogh Escalation
concepts.summary: Frontier models incur sticker shock in an agentic loop for two compounding reasons — queued latency and multi-turn token consumption — and the fix is climbing the escalation ladder deliberately, painting a stick figure before attempting a Van Gogh.

concepts.title: Non-Stationarity and CTDE: Why Multi-Agent Worlds Move While You Reason
concepts.summary: A multi-agent environment changes for reasons unrelated to your own actions, invalidating the single-agent assumption that made earlier RL math tractable — Centralized Training, Decentralized Execution is the industry's answer, trained like a master chef overseeing many independent cooks.

concepts.title: Reward Hacking and Credit Assignment When the Team Is the Agent
concepts.summary: Multi-agent teams exploit the exact letter of a shared reward function faster and more creatively than any single agent, and the Advantage Function's job — was this action better than average, given the team's global outcome — gets structurally harder once "average" spans multiple cooperating or competing agents.

concepts.title: The Multi-Turn Reliability Gap: Why Untrained Agents Fail 70% of the Time
concepts.summary: A multi-step agentic task compounds per-step stochastic error rates multiplicatively, and this arithmetic — not any single dramatic bug — is why untrained agents attempting realistic workflows like flight booking succeed only about 30% of the time.

concepts.title: Agent Lightning: Automatic Tracing, Equal Credit, and GRPO for Real Agents
concepts.summary: Agent Lightning turns any agent's execution into RL training data automatically, uses a deliberately crude equal-credit strategy that the law of large numbers cleans up statistically, and GRPO's group-relative normalization keeps training stable when a single agent juggles wildly different reward scales.
